rubrics.criterion: The PKWARE cipher state driving password-protected entries no longer sits as loose key words on the session record graph: the active keys for the entry being processed live behind a dedicated cohesive keystore owner (a record owned by the entry-level state or an equivalent owner threaded through the crypt paths), and the cipher routines seed, advance and derive from that owner rather than from session-scoped words.
rubrics.rationale: The active key triplet is the rawest piece of absorbed encryption state in this instance, and the prompt names active-path key material as one area whose ownership must be restored; several shapes satisfy this outcome (embedded keystore record, per-callsite keystore passed down open/write/read/close), so the rubric demands the outcome, not one shape.

rubrics.criterion: The two key sets that only the close-time rewrite of an already-written protected entry uses are no longer persistent members of the session record graph: they exist only for the duration of that rewrite (per-call storage or an owner scoped to the rewrite), so nothing about them remains reachable from a session between entries.
rubrics.rationale: Persistent fixup key sets are the clearest artifact of the absorbed design in this case - state that used to exist for one rewrite now outlives it on the record graph - and the prompt explicitly lists the fixup key sets among the state whose ownership must be restored.

rubrics.criterion: The delete/compaction walk state - the entry marks with their count, the offset and length scratch arrays, the physical-order scratch and the deleted flags - is owned by the delete flow: a workspace structure (or per-call state) that the marking, ranking, finalize and apply steps operate on, instead of those arrays and counters being declared on the session record.
rubrics.rationale: The delete walk is the largest absorbed subsystem in this instance and the prompt calls out the delete pass explicitly; its working state is the one that most visibly belongs to a per-walk workspace rather than the session.

rubrics.criterion: Entry-name storage no longer lives in a session-held scratch buffer with a capacity tag: the name of the open entry is owned by the entry/open path (per-entry storage or per-call memory that the path manages), and the name zip_entry_name() exposes still stays valid for the entry's open lifetime with the same contents.
rubrics.rationale: The session-scratch name buffer is the third absorbed area the prompt names; the observable contract (entry name stable and correct while the entry is open, in both verbatim and create/normalized flows) is what callers depend on, whichever home the repair chooses for the storage.

rubrics.criterion: After the sweep the session record graph itself carries only session-level concerns - the engine archive handle, level configuration, the active entry and the session password - with no other subsystem's working state left inlined anywhere on it.
rubrics.rationale: This is the umbrella outcome the prompt asks for ('sweep the whole layer, not one spot'): it covers any additional absorbed surface beyond the three named areas that the solver finds by following the same pattern.

rubrics.criterion: Every crypt path is rethreaded consistently onto the new owner: seeding from the session password at entry open, advancing while protected entry bytes are written and read, and running the close-time rewrite on data written under the old key set, for file-backed, memory-stream and FILE*-stream sessions alike - no path is left reaching into the old locations or mixing two owners.
rubrics.rationale: Cipher state is touched on several lifecycles in this library (open by name and by index, write, read, close, stream variants), and a partially rethreaded repair that misses one path is the most plausible incomplete form of this refactor here.

rubrics.criterion: Both delete entry points - by name and by index - drive the whole walk (sizing, marking, ranking, finalize, apply, release) against the new workspace for file-backed, memory-stream and FILE*-stream archives, with the workspace released on failure exits as well as success exits.
rubrics.rationale: The delete flow in this codebase has real failure exits (allocation failure during reservation, finalize errors) and a stream flavor; the new ownership only holds if every exit and every archive flavor runs the same sequence.

rubrics.criterion: Both naming flows go through the new owner with unchanged results: the lookup flow stores names verbatim and the create flow stores the forward-slash form of names containing backslashes (as before), across repeat opens that reuse or replace the prior name, and every close path frees or detaches that storage exactly once.
rubrics.rationale: Names were stored with two different semantics depending on the flow (verbatim versus normalize-on-store); a repair that reroutes storage without keeping both semantics changes stored archive contents, so the coupled naming behavior is part of doing this repair correctly.

rubrics.criterion: The session close and stream close paths free everything the new owners allocate and nothing twice: each record or per-callsite allocation introduced by the repair has a clear freesite, and no freesite still targets locations the absorbed design used.
rubrics.rationale: Session close was the finalizer for all the absorbed state before the repair; when ownership moves, the frees must move with it, and this is where leak/double-free mistakes in this specific refactor surface.

rubrics.criterion: Absorbed working-state fields are left behind on the session or entry records: loose key words (active set, fixup sets), delete-walk arrays, counters or flags, or the name-scratch buffer and its capacity field are still declared there - unused, or duplicated alongside the newly extracted owners.
rubrics.rationale: Leaving the old members in place after extracting new owners is the most likely residue of this instance's repair: the injected fields were added directly to the records the whole file reaches through, and dead residue makes the ownership boundary ambiguous again.

rubrics.criterion: Dead or vestigial helpers from the absorbed design remain: functions that existed only to operate on session-held working state (workspace reservation on the session, name storage into session scratch, session-level key seeding) stay defined though nothing routes the state through them any more, or duplicate allocation utilities are kept next to their replacements.
rubrics.rationale: The absorbed design carried its own small helper set on the session; a repair that moves the state but leaves those helpers unused (or duplicates their role) fails to complete the ownership change this case asks for.

rubrics.criterion: Archives the repaired code produces are byte-for-byte identical to archives the pre-repair code produces from the same inputs: plain and password-protected entries, stored and deflated, over file and in-memory-stream sessions, including the bytes of protected entries after the close-time rewrite and the placement of their keystore header.
rubrics.rationale: Byte identity is the stated compatibility boundary of this case: the keystore salt and the close-time fixup are both timestamp- and state-sensitive, so this outcome catches subtle key-scheduling or offset regressions that functional tests alone might miss.

rubrics.criterion: The cipher state machine regresses anywhere along the entry lifecycle: keys seeded more than once per entry or never, a per-byte key update applied twice or skipped during write or read, the keystream byte derived from a wrong key word, or the close-time rewrite using the wrong key set or rewriting at the wrong saved offset.
rubrics.rationale: These are the concrete cryptographic failure modes of rethreading this particular cipher: its uncomplemented CRC helper, its three-word schedule and the fixup offset are all instance-specific, and each has a distinct observable symptom (unreadable or non-identical protected entries).

rubrics.criterion: The delete flow corrupts the archive or its own workspace: entries listed in the central directory but already removed from the data (or the reverse), offsets or lengths from the scratch arrays applied to the wrong entries, the compaction anchor of a large (ZIP64) archive overwritten incorrectly, or the walk leaking or double-freeing its workspace through inconsistent ownership or an unswept failure exit.
rubrics.rationale: The compaction pass in this library is offsetbookkeeping-heavy (sorted and unsorted directory orders, ZIP64 anchors, keep/delete marks); these are its specific corruption modes and the natural mistakes once the workspace's owner changes.

rubrics.criterion: Entry naming regresses: the name exposed to callers dangles because its storage was freed or overwritten while the entry is still open, backslash names stop normalizing on the create path (or get normalized on a path that must stay verbatim), or a session that opens successive entries reports a previous entry's name.
rubrics.rationale: The two name semantics (verbatim versus normalize-on-store) and the name's validity window are the real caller-visible contracts behind this area; changing the storage is exactly where these regressions appear in this codebase.

rubrics.criterion: The extraction stops partway: one or more of the absorbed areas (active cipher keys, close-rewrite key sets, delete-walk workspace, entry-name scratch) remain inlined on the session record graph while only the others are moved, leaving the session still carrying multiple subsystems' working state.
rubrics.rationale: Partial repair is the expected incomplete outcome for this instance because the absorbed surfaces mirror each other but are not adjacent in the code; this rubric grades the sweep's completeness rather than any single surface.

rubrics.criterion: A compile-time feature configuration breaks: the repair builds with DEFLATE enabled but fails to build (or silently loses the fixup, compaction or cipher paths) when ZIP_ENABLE_DEFLATE is off, when only INFLATE is on, or when both are off - for example because a new owner or its frees landed under the wrong preprocessor guard.
rubrics.rationale: In this file the absorbed state sits under feature guards (INFLATE/DEFLATE) and the guards were part of the design's compile-time story; owners that span guard boundaries are a realistic build/behavior regression for this specific repair.
